title: Website Redesign URL Inventory: What to Keep, Redirect or Retire
description: Build a practical URL inventory before a website redesign, then decide which pages to keep, update, merge, redirect or retire.
summary: Protect useful pages and visitor journeys during a redesign with a URL inventory, decision framework and downloadable redirect worksheet.
body:
A website redesign can improve the offer, structure and editing experience while accidentally removing pages that customers, search engines or campaigns still use. A visual page list is not enough. Before new routes are approved, build an inventory of the current URLs and give each one a documented destination.

This is a planning task for website redesign services in India and elsewhere. It does not predict rankings. It helps the business and delivery team agree what survives, what changes and how each decision will be tested.

Build the inventory from more than the menu

The main navigation shows only the pages someone chose to feature. Older landing pages, downloads, form thank-you pages and campaign URLs may be absent from it while still receiving visits or links.

Start with the current sitemap and content management system. Add URLs found in analytics, Search Console, server logs, internal links, campaign records and saved business documents. Include useful PDFs, images or other files that need to move. Record the evidence source beside every row so the team can investigate gaps instead of assuming the list is complete.

Google’s site-move guidance recommends starting with important URLs from sitemaps, traffic records and links, then mapping old URLs to new destinations for more complex moves.

Give every old URL one clear decision

A practical decision framework for each current URL
DecisionWhen it fitsAcceptance check
KeepThe purpose, content and address remain useful.The live page still works and the new site links to it where relevant.
UpdateThe page keeps its purpose but needs clearer content, design or functionality.The address resolves normally and the approved changes are present.
MoveThe same useful page receives a new address.The old address permanently redirects to the matching new page.
MergeTwo or more pages serve the same visitor task and a combined page is more useful.Each old address redirects directly to the relevant combined destination.
RetireThe content has no useful replacement and should be removed.The response and visitor message match the agreed retirement plan; no important internal links remain.

A redirect is not a substitute for deciding whether the new page satisfies the old visitor intent. Avoid sending unrelated discontinued pages to the homepage. Google warns that redirecting many old URLs to one irrelevant destination can confuse users and may be treated as a soft 404.

Hypothetical example: a Varanasi home-maintenance business

Imagine a fictional Varanasi home-maintenance business redesigning a six-year-old website. This is an original planning example, not a SiteSutra client engagement or a performance claim.

The inventory finds a live plumbing service page, an electrical-repair page linked from an old directory listing, two duplicate contact pages and a PDF price list that the business no longer honours. The new structure keeps the two service pages at clearer addresses, combines the contact routes into one enquiry page and retires the outdated PDF without redirecting it to an unrelated page.

The team records the old and new addresses, the business reason, the redirect type and the acceptance test. Before launch, it checks that service buttons reach the intended enquiry route. After launch, it requests each old URL and confirms the response reaches the final destination without an unnecessary redirect chain.

Choose redirects from the business decision

When a page has permanently moved to an equivalent destination, Google recommends server-side permanent redirects such as HTTP 301 or 308 where possible. Its redirect documentation explains that permanent and temporary redirects send different canonical signals.

Record the intended response instead of writing only “redirect.” A temporary campaign change may need different handling from a permanent redesign route. Point the old URL directly to its final destination where possible. A chain adds another request for visitors and creates another place for the route to fail.

Update the new site as well as the old routes

  • Change internal links so they point directly to the final new URLs.
  • Give indexable new pages self-referencing canonical links.
  • Update navigation, XML sitemaps, structured data, hreflang annotations when used, and campaign destinations.
  • Move approved downloads and media that visitors still need.
  • Check that launch-only noindex rules or crawler blocks are removed from public pages.

A sitemap should contain the preferred canonical URLs. Google describes sitemap submission as a hint rather than a guarantee of crawling or indexing in its sitemap guidance.

Test the map as a launch acceptance item

For each moved URL, record the actual response, final destination and result. Test important enquiry, booking, download and service journeys on the production host. Check that the new canonical names the intended public address and that the page remains accessible without animation or client-side navigation.

Keep the redirect map after launch. Google recommends retaining redirects for as long as possible, generally at least one year for site moves. Continue to review not-found responses, submitted sitemap URLs and important pages in Search Console. Search visibility, sampled AI citations and qualified enquiries remain separate measurements.

Download the URL inventory and redirect worksheet

Download the website redesign URL inventory (CSV). It includes clearly labelled hypothetical rows plus blank fields for the current purpose, evidence source, decision, new URL, redirect status, internal-link update, canonical check, sitemap action, owner and test result.

Replace the examples with verified information from your website. Do not include passwords, customer messages or private analytics exports in a shared worksheet.

Make the URL map part of the redesign scope

Ask the redesign provider who builds the inventory, who approves each destination, who implements the routes and what evidence completes acceptance. A useful proposal names these responsibilities before development begins.
